contributions.headingText: A teratoma with somatic-type malignancy is a teratoma that develops a distinct component that resembles a somatic-type malignant neoplasm (e.g. sarcoma, carcinoma), as seen in other organs and tissues.
2C80.4 & XH33E8 Malignant teratoma of testis & Teratoma with malignant transformation
Not recommended: teratoma with malignant transformation; teratoma with a secondary malignant component.

Somatic-type malignancies occur in 2.5–8.0% of testicular germ cell tumours {17261854; 2990657; 21134986; 6090001}, virtually only in postpubertal patients (ranging in age from 15 to 68 years) {21134986; 24921638; 9400455}. Most patients have teratomatous germ cell tumours {21134986; 9400455; 24952240}; however, a recent study suggested that many somatic-type sarcomas actually arise from yolk sac tumours {25229769; 33136584}. The somatic-type malignancies associated with teratoma most commonly occur in retroperitoneal lymph nodes seen in resections after cisplatin-based chemotherapy; they occur less commonly in primary testicular germ cell tumour and at other metastatic sites {2990657; 24921638}. The interval from the diagnosis of a germ cell tumour to the onset of a somatic-type malignancy varies widely; some malignancies are seen in the primary site and others occur > 30 years later {32381397}. Carcinomas develop late in the course of disease (median: 108 months from germ cell tumour diagnosis), whereas sarcomas develop earlier (median: 20 months) {24952240}.

There are no distinct features ascribed to somatic-type malignancies. The sarcomas may appear as solid, whitish-grey to tan, firm, nodular masses; however, in the presence of teratoma it is not possible to distinguish them with certainty.

Depending on the type of malignancy, the tumours may display expansile or infiltrative growth patterns. To declare a tumour as a somatic-type malignancy, the tumours should exhibit a pure population of atypical mesenchymal or epithelial cells and occupy at least one low-power field (×4 objective, 5 mm in diameter) {6090001}. However, the tumour may be separated by foci of teratoma and other germ cell tumour components, and less stringent criteria may be applied because the overall amount of tumour may exceed 5 mm in contiguous sections. Teratoma often displays marked atypia, consists of somewhat organoid admixtures of varied elements, and is often mixed with other germ cell tumour components. Radiation and chemotherapy may also induce atypical changes in both neoplastic and supportive cells, but treatment-induced atypia is usually diffuse and lacks the requisite nodular or infiltrative growth of a single type of atypical cell population {3024806}. Sarcomas are more common than carcinomas and often appear early in the course of the disease. It is of utmost importance that these malignancies be differentiated from teratoma because their presence dramatically impacts prognosis and overall survival.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most commonly identified sarcoma in postchemotherapy resections {19561445; 17721191; 9400455; 24921638}. It represents more than half of all sarcomas {17721191; 19561445}. The majority of these are embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, whereas alveolar and pleomorphic subtypes occur occasionally. Approximately 50% of patients were disease-free after a median follow-up of 75 months {21134986; 19561445; 9400455}. Leiomyosarcoma, angiosarcoma, and other sarcomas are infrequently reported {19561445; 17721191}.

Embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumour (formerly “primitive neuroectodermal tumour”) is another relatively common somatic-type malignancy for which WHO has adopted new terminology {6314925; 9255252}. These tumours represent an overgrowth of embryonic-type neuroectodermal tissue that is commonly seen in teratomas and often categorized as an immature neuroectodermal component. They resemble CNS embryonal tumours and lack the chromosome 22 translocation seen in peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumours (Ewing sarcoma) {20348883}. The change in terminology was necessary because these tumours are often referred to as “central-type primitive neuroectodermal tumours”; however, the current WHO classification for the CNS does not contain this term because these and similar primitive tumours were classified under the category of embryonal tumours in the 2016 WHO classification. This change provides alignment with CNS terminology and will help avoid the misinterpretation of this tumour as Ewing sarcoma, which has vastly different therapeutic implications. Embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumours often show glial differentiation, more commonly in postchemotherapy instances. If the predominant glial component is present, it is pertinent to classify it as glioma or glioblastoma multiforme if it displays anaplastic features. GFAP, S100, and SOX11 are positive in the tumour cells {33290506}.

Rarely, nephroblastoma may develop in a teratoma {9737244} or occur in pure form {7529549} in metastasis.

Most carcinomas are adenocarcinomas (usually NOS) {24921638}. Squamous cell, neuroendocrine, and poorly differentiated carcinomas have also been found in teratomas {21134986; 24921638; 9400455}. Rarely, two types of secondary somatic-type malignancies develop simultaneously {9474169; 23784825}. Somatic-type malignancies demonstrate immunohistochemical features similar to those of their counterparts in other organs. They generally lose immunoreactivity for PLAP, OCT3/4, and AFP, but they may maintain various degrees of positivity for SALL4 {24921638}. Although most neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) develop from prepubertal-type teratomas, some are associated with germ cell neoplasia in situ and isochromosome 12p and therefore arise from postpubertal-type teratomas {18316560}.
Cytomorphological features in metastasis may help in determining the presence of epithelial or sarcomatous malignancy.

Isochromosome 12p and overrepresentation of 12p has been demonstrated in most somatic-type malignancies {23154771; 9400455; 31478941}. Chromosomal rearrangements analogous to their counterparts in other locations have also been shown {9400455}. Two thirds of somatic-type malignancies have patterns of loss of heterozygosity identical to those of their matched teratomas, and the remaining ones showed additional allelic losses {14633619; 23154771}.

Essential: expansile and infiltrative growth of epithelial or mesenchymal component measuring ≥ 5 mm.

Desirable: specific somatic features and immunohistochemistry are helpful in most cases.
Staging follows the 2018 Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) and American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM classification.

The prognosis is generally not affected if the somatic malignancy is not the predominant component and confined to the testis {19561445; 9400455}. However, in metastasis or recurrence, mortality risk is increased {19561445; 9400455}. The histological type does not seem to be an independent prognostic factor in multivariate analysis {24952240}. If the malignancy is localized, surgical resection is the treatment of choice {20868391}. Patients with somatic-type malignancies respond poorly to the cisplatin-based chemotherapy used for conventional germ cell tumour {21134986; 9400455}; however, some may respond to specific chemotherapy that is effective for their counterpart in other organs {14645417}.
